cards.front: Kernicterus is caused by the [___] fraction of bilirubin, which is lipid-soluble, poorly albumin-bound at high levels, and able to cross the neonatal blood-brain barrier.
cards.context:
This is the same fraction that rises in haemolysis (Rh/ABO, G6PD), which is why jaundice in the first 24 h is treated as a haemolytic emergency.

A raised conjugated (direct) fraction is a different problem — it does not cross the blood-brain barrier, is never physiological, and points to biliary atresia or neonatal hepatitis.

Trap: reading any neonatal jaundice as benign.

cards.front: Severe hypertension in pregnancy means systolic ≥[___] or diastolic ≥110 mmHg.
cards.context:
NSW ACI 2026: systolic ≥160 OR diastolic ≥110 mmHg is severe hypertension. Confirmation uses three consecutive measurements at least two minutes apart.

Severe hypertension requires immediate escalation and treatment; do not wait for both numbers to cross the threshold.

cards.front: A Bishop score of [___] means the cervix is favourable, so induction can start with amniotomy with or without oxytocin.
cards.context:
Australian units use the modified Bishop score: cervical length in cm replaces effacement. Dilatation, length and station score 0-3; consistency and position 0-2. QCG calls 7 or more favourable.

Ripening options: prostaglandin (PGE2 dinoprostone gel/pessary, or misoprostol PGE1), cervical balloon (Foley or Cook), or membrane sweeping for borderline.

Failed induction is more common with low scores. Australian guidance ripens the cervix at 6 or less; US sources often quote 8 as the cut-off.

cards.front: At 23 weeks, a fetus develops hydrops and Doppler evidence of anaemia. Maternal antibody screening is negative. Several weeks earlier, the mother had arthralgia after her child developed a slapped-cheek rash. The most likely infecting virus is [___].
cards.context:
Parvovirus infects fetal erythroid precursors, reducing red-cell production and potentially causing high-output failure with hydrops.

The exposure and maternal arthralgia support infection; a negative red-cell antibody screen makes alloimmune haemolysis less likely.

cards.front: Because multiple pregnancy is a listed fetal risk factor, Queensland intrapartum fetal surveillance guidance recommends continuous [___] in active labour.
cards.context:
Twins are on the fetal risk list in their own right, so no extra risk factor is needed before continuous monitoring is recommended.

The guidance does not by itself set the timing or mode of birth.

cards.front: In antepartum haemorrhage, digital vaginal examination is avoided until ultrasound has excluded [___].
cards.context:
A finger through the cervix can provoke catastrophic bleeding from a praevia. Check the placental site on the morphology scan report or with ultrasound first.

A gentle speculum examination is acceptable to look for a cervical cause and estimate loss.

cards.front: A woman in front of you after a sensitising bleed is offered anti-D within [___] hours.
cards.context: Offer anti-D within 72 hours of a sensitising bleed, and do not delay if she is in front of you. Anti-D binds fetal cells before the mother starts her own immune response.

cards.front: At a 10-week booking visit with her GP, a woman whose last pregnancy was complicated by pre-eclampsia asks how to lower her risk of pre-eclampsia this time. The GP should start aspirin [___] mg daily at night.
cards.context:
Previous pre-eclampsia is the strongest clinical risk factor in the Queensland table, about eight times the baseline risk. Aspirin is started early, ideally before 16 weeks, and taken at night.

It reduces pre-eclampsia, small-for-gestational-age babies and preterm birth.

cards.front: The Safer Baby Bundle's five elements are smoking cessation, detection of [___], awareness of decreased fetal movements, side-sleeping from 28 weeks, and individualised timing of birth.
cards.context:
The bundle combines risk reduction, early recognition of fetal compromise and shared decisions.

Birth timing reflects each woman's risks and preferences; it is not a fixed early-delivery rule.

cards.front: A pregnant woman asks her GP about treating nausea and vomiting with cannabis. She is advised against it: cannabis use in pregnancy is associated with preterm birth and lower [___].
cards.context:
Cannabis, including medicinal cannabinoids, is not recommended during pregnancy. Cannabinoids cross the placenta.

Observational studies link use with lower birthweight, preterm birth and neonatal unit admission; tobacco co-use confounds, so causation is uncertain. Antiemetics with safety data are offered instead.

cards.front: Trial of labour after caesarean: baseline uterine rupture risk is approximately 0.5% in experienced centres; risk [___] with oxytocin augmentation. Overall TOLAC success rate is around 70%.
cards.context:
VBAC carries a small but real risk of uterine rupture along the previous scar — ~1:200 (0.5%) in experienced centres for a single previous transverse lower segment CS.

Risk doubles with oxytocin augmentation (over-stimulation stresses scar), rises with prior classical (vertical) incision (~5-10% — generally contraindicates VBAC), multiple previous CS.

VBAC success rate ~70%, lower without prior vaginal birth + recurrent CS indication.

cards.front: HPV vaccination prevents about 90% of cervical cancers; the nonavalent vaccine covers [___] oncogenic HPV types.
cards.context:
The nonavalent vaccine covers seven oncogenic types (16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58) plus the low-risk wart types 6 and 11.

Vaccinated women therefore still need screening to catch the residual risk.

The National Cervical Screening Program runs 5-yearly HPV testing from 25 to 74 regardless of vaccination; any oncogenic HPV gets reflex liquid-based cytology, and HPV 16/18 goes to colposcopy.

cards.front: For postpartum haemorrhage, start tranexamic acid as soon as possible and within [___] of birth.
cards.context: WHO recommends 1 g IV over 10 minutes within three hours of birth, alongside resuscitation and cause-directed treatment. Do not delay it until uterotonics fail.

cards.front: With a normal hip examination but DDH risk factors, screening hip [___] is commonly arranged at about 6 weeks; confirmed DDH may be treated with a specialist-directed Pavlik harness.
cards.context:
With normal examination but breech presentation or first-degree family history, use the local screening pathway. An unstable newborn hip needs prompt senior/orthopaedic assessment, not delayed screening.

Treatment depends on confirmed findings and age. A Pavlik harness is one specialist-directed option in young infants. [RCH DDH](https://www.rch.org.au/uploadedFiles/Main/Content/ortho/factsheets/DDH.pdf).

cards.front: Jaundice appearing in the first 24 hours particularly raises concern for [___].
cards.context:
Jaundice before 24 hours is pathological until assessed; consider Rh/ABO haemolysis. Check maternal/baby blood groups, DAT, FBC/film, reticulocytes and serum bilirubin.

Use age-, gestation- and risk-specific treatment charts: phototherapy first, exchange transfusion at its threshold or for bilirubin encephalopathy. IV fluids support hydration; they do not replace treatment.

cards.front: For a woman, a BMI of 30 kg/m² before pregnancy is the threshold defining [___].
cards.context: The threshold classifies BMI and does not create a sudden biological change in risk. Higher BMI is associated with gestational diabetes, hypertensive disease, thrombosis and stillbirth.
